passages.heading_path: INC-2288: Sustained CPU from an OS denial-analysis daemon
passages.text: Summary A denial-analysis daemon held roughly 20% CPU sustained on mid-prod-f3 for six days, spiking to full utilisation during filesystem scans. Signature Detected under the stable signature `host.cpu.saturation:mid-prod-f3`. Timeline - **D0, 03:00** Denial volume rises sharply. The audit dispatcher starts the analysis daemon, which stays resident. Source: audit log. - **D+6, 14:20** Daemon identified in a process snapshot as the top CPU consumer. Source: bridge. - **D+6, 15:05** Audit event dispatcher deactivated. Daemon exits and CPU recovers. Source: host. Resolution Deactivated the audit
passages.cause_claimed: Denial volume from a policy change kept the OS denial-analysis daemon resident and busy.
passages.superseded_by: Platform security standard SEC-STD-14 (2026-01-30) requires the audit event dispatcher to remain active on production hosts. Deactivating it is no longer an available resolution, and doing it here destroyed the evidence that would have identified the source domain.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: correlating change against onset
passages.text: Run this first, not last Package history and change records against the onset time is a lookup, not an investigation. It costs one command and one registry query. It is routinely run hours into a bridge, after the expensive hypotheses have already been formed and defended. Run it before the first hypothesis, so the board starts from what changed rather than from what someone remembered. Correlation is not attribution The most recent change on a host is the most available explanation, not the most likely one. Availability is why the newest component gets named first, and why it is often the one

passages.heading_path: Runbook: correlating change against onset
passages.text: with a representative on the call. A change that correlates in time earns a place on the hypothesis board with its confidence stated and a falsifying test attached. It does not earn a cause. Absence of change is not absence of change Components that update themselves outside the package manager do not appear in package history with a current timestamp. An empty result means the query found nothing, which is not the same as nothing having happened. Record the query, its window, and what it cannot see. A correlation report that does not state its blind spots reads as complete when it is not.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: correlating change against onset
passages.text: What to carry forward For each correlated change: what changed, when, who implemented it, the interval to onset, and the single piece of evidence that would rule it out. The interval alone is not a ranking.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: collecting the security denial log
passages.text: What this evidence settles A denial log names the source domain of each denial. That is what separates one candidate process from another when several are plausible and none has been ruled out. Without it, every candidate stays equally likely and the investigation converges on whichever party has someone available to answer. It is usually a single command and a few seconds of host access. The cost of collecting it is almost never the reason it goes uncollected. Collect before suppressing Deactivating the event dispatcher stops the denials reaching analysis, which is often proposed as relief

passages.heading_path: Runbook: collecting the security denial log
passages.text: when a denial-analysis process is consuming CPU. It also stops the log being collectable. If suppression is applied before the log is taken, the evidence that would have identified the source is gone, and no later collection recovers it. Collect first, then suppress if suppression is still wanted. Runtime changes revert on reboot Setting the enforcement mode at runtime does not change the boot configuration. The host will return to its configured mode on the next restart, which may be months away and will not be associated with this incident by anyone who was not on the call. Any proposal to

passages.heading_path: Runbook: collecting the security denial log
passages.text: change enforcement mode must state whether it is runtime only, and any record of it must say the same. If the log cannot be produced Record it as outstanding deciding evidence, name what each outcome would rule in and rule out, and leave the hypothesis unresolved. A request that was made twice and never satisfied is a finding about the investigation, and it belongs in the record.

passages.heading_path: Runbook: host memory exhaustion
passages.text: When this applies A host is reported as memory exhausted, swapping, or showing an elevated page fault rate. It applies whether or not an alert has fired, and whether or not anyone has acknowledged one. Establish the standing condition first Find the resident set of the largest existing consumer and compare it against total memory. A host that normally runs at ninety per cent of memory is not the same incident as a host that normally runs at forty and has just moved. The standing condition is not the cause. It is what decides whether a new consumer of a given size is enough to matter. Record it

passages.heading_path: Runbook: host memory exhaustion
passages.text: as a condition, not as a finding. Attribute the memory before changing anything Take a process-level snapshot while the host is still exhausted. Resident set by process, ordered, with start times. A snapshot taken after a restart proves nothing, and the restart is the most common way this evidence is destroyed. If the snapshot cannot be taken, record that as a gap rather than proceeding as though the attribution is known. Distinguish a new consumer from a changed one Two shapes present identically. Either a process that was not there before has arrived, or an existing process has changed

passages.heading_path: Runbook: host memory exhaustion
passages.text: behaviour. The start time in the process snapshot separates them, and they have nothing in common beyond the symptom. A new consumer points at change history. A changed consumer points at the dependency or destination that changed underneath it. What not to do Do not raise a memory limit to relieve pressure before the consumer is attributed. Raising a limit consumes the headroom that a correct attribution would need, and it can convert an intermittent condition into a permanent one. Do not restart the workload as a first step. It resolves the symptom and destroys the evidence in the same

passages.heading_path: Runbook: selecting a recovery point during an incident
passages.text: The window matters more than the age A recovery point taken inside the affected window restores the condition along with the host. The snapshot will restore cleanly, validate against every check that does not look for the condition, and reproduce the incident. Before selecting a point, establish when the condition began. If onset is not known, treat every point after the first unexplained symptom as suspect. Rehearsal is not validation A restore that completes is not a restore that works. Time the restore, then run the workload's own checks against the restored copy. A rehearsal that stops at

passages.heading_path: Runbook: selecting a recovery point during an incident
passages.text: "the restore completed" has measured the storage layer and nothing above it. Record the elapsed time against the stated expectation. A restore that takes significantly longer than the expectation is a finding whether or not the data is correct. What to record The recovery point selected, the onset time it was checked against, the elapsed restore time against the expectation, and what validation was run. A rehearsal with no recorded validation is an untested assumption with a timestamp on it.
